Ok this may be long. I'm going to be brief as possible, just ask if you need clarification.

Traditional oil reservoirs are actually made of sand. They have a high permeability. Permeability measures how easily the oil can flow through. The typical process is (very simple explanation) get a pipe in the ground, put holes in it and let the oil flow up that pipe to the surface.

Fracking is a relatively new technology. "Fracking" stands for hydraulic fracturing. This gives them the ability to produce reservoirs that are not able to be used because they don't have enough permeability. The drilling process is the same, but instead of just putting holes in the pipe and letting the oil flow, they have to make the reservoir more permeable. They do this by pushing "fracking" fluids into the reservoir at extremely high pressures to break the rock in the reservoir and make it more permeable, and therefore economic to produce.

I'm putting this a separate comment to discuss the environmental concerns.

There's already plenty of pushback over typical oil wells and oil production. Fracking adds in an hugely increased use of water, some chemicals being injected in the ground, and the threat of the fracturing getting out of control and basically opening channels between water tables (drinking water) and oil reservoirs. There is also some debate on if fracking is causing a larger and larger earthquake threat.

Most oil and has historically been taken from certain areas where it all stays in one place. Certain pockets where a lot (thousands or millions of barrels) all trapped in a single bubble which once you drill into you can release it at once. Fracking instead looks for areas of rock where there is a lot of oil and gas but it's not in a single bubble, it's in many small bubbles over a large area. Instead of drilling one hole in the middle and sucking it out, you make a well and push a liquid down at high pressure to break the rock between these bubbles. The rock fractured rock sinks to the bottom and you then have a bigger bubble with oil/gas than you started with. Repeat this again and again and you can get a lot of oil out of these fracking fields. Advantages; Oil and gas, you don't have to buy from overseas. Jobs, infrastructure etc etc.

Disadvantages; Oil and gas, we need to cut down on our use, not find more to burn. No one really knows what is in the "liquid" that is pumped down the well as it seems to be trade secrets. That liquid if not disposed of properly or left in the emptied wells may become a contaminate above ground. People say there is a risk of earthquakes, and fracking really does cause earthquakes, but they're small on a par with a dump truck going past your house.

"Trickle Down Theory" and "Tax Cuts for the Rich" by Thomas Sowell (Conservative Professor of Economics, Stanford)

"Implicit in the approach of both academic and media critics of what they call “tax cuts for the rich” and a “trickle-down theory” is a zero- sum conception of the economy, where the benefits of some come at the expense of others."

Here, Sowell creates a classic straw man - an imagined enemy which is designed for him to easily defeat.

Most of the criticism of "trickle down" I've seen has strongly flatly rejected a "zero sum game." Most of the criticism I've seen has revolved around the idea that more funds in the hands of the poor has a much more stimulative effect on the economy than putting more money into the hands of the rich. These discussions usually go into detail as to why giving money to the poor stimulates the economy, resulting in a (non-zero-sum) gain which is then spread out into the wider economy. For example:

If you give a poor person (or even someone in the middle class) $5,000, they will spend it, directly infusing capital into jobs which are again stimulative (thus rapidly providing several waves of economic stimulus)

On the other hand, if you give a "bonus" $5,000 (via tax breaks or whatever means) to a person with $200 million in net worth, they will invest it - sometimes offshore, and sometimes in low-economic-return activity like rapid stock trading (which has little positive impact on the economy outside of providing a marginally more efficient market in which to trade stock)

Of course investment anywhere can create some economic stimulus, but the argument here isn't that all investment is pointless, but rather that the economic advantages of pumping money into investment versus stimulating spending are obvious. At the store front (and service industry) level, for example, one can ask a manager:

If demand for goods remained the same, and you made $1 million in additional **profits **this year - would you hire more workers? A good manager would say "no" (unless the business is already woefully short-staffed)

But ask this way:

If **demand **increased such that the marginal utility of adding employees would indicate that you should hire more workers - would you hire more workers? A good manager would say "yes."

The best takedown of the "trickle-down" myth I've ever read:

What free-marketeers in fact advocate is not trickle-down, but trickle-up. The way to become rich, in a competitive economy, is to offer a service to the broad mass of consumers. I am typing these words using software that I bought from Bill Gates. The transaction enriched him – adding fractionally to his net wealth – but it also enriched me, making my life more convenient. Bill Gates became wealthy, in other words, by persuading a great many poorer people to buy something from him. In doing so, he made us considerably better off, too. Trickle-up, you see.

Trickle-down, by contrast, would represent the precise opposite of an open market system. It would involve handing wads of cash to the undeserving rich in the hope that their affluence would somehow transfer itself to the rest of us. Now such transfers do occasionally happen. The bank bailouts were the most notorious example: they shifted a great deal of money, through coercive taxation, from people on low and medium incomes to wealthy bankers and bondholders. The Common Agricultural Policy is another instance: its cost falls disproportionately on the poor, who spend a relatively high percentage of their income on food, and its benefits go overwhelmingly to big landowners. Likewise the alternative energy boondoggles that force the general population to subsidise those same landowners through higher fuel bills.

Every free-marketeer I know opposes these rackets. We dislike subsidies, whether for the rich or for anyone else. We know that, for all its imperfections, the open economy is the best way to generate wealth across the board. The poor get richer and, yes, the rich do, too. Over time, on average, we all trickle up. I’m still waiting to hear of a better alternative.
